title: The Peal perfect

objectives.can: Recognise a Peal perfect and give its person, gender and number.
Recognise ten of the commonest verbs.

explanation.summary: The perfect of the Peal is the form of a verb that tells what was done. It is the commonest narrative verb form in the Aramaic of Daniel and Ezra, and its ending shows the person, gender and number of the subject. This lesson teaches the endings and what the texts hold of them.

sections.heading: Stem and ending
body: A Peal perfect is the root with a short vowel pattern, followed by an ending. The pattern is usually a shewa under the first consonant and a under the second: אֲמַר 'he said', יְהַב 'he gave', נְפַל 'he fell', עֲבַד 'he made'. The ending then adds the subject. For the third-person masculine singular there is no ending at all, which is why the dictionary lists the verb by that form.
Some verbs, many of which describe a state or a bodily action, have another vowel in the second syllable: שְׁאֵל 'he asked', סְגִד 'he did homage', קְרֵב 'he approached'. The endings are the same.

The perfect usually presents an action as complete, and in narrative it commonly tells what happened. It does not mean 'past' in every use, and the time of a verb is judged from its sentence. Do not translate it by rule.

sections.heading: The endings
body: The table gives the endings as they are written in the Aramaic of the Bible. A hyphen shows where the ending joins the stem. Where the texts have a form for a person and number, the lesson cites a real word; where they have none, the table says so. Biblical Aramaic is a small body of text, and no second-person feminine form and no second-person feminine plural stands in it.

Verbs whose last root consonant is weak (those which end in a vowel, like עֲנָה 'he answered' and חֲזָא 'he saw') build their forms a little differently. For example the first person singular is חֲזֵית and the third person masculine plural is עֲנוֹ. These are met again in A3.1. Here it is enough to know that the endings below are the regular ones and that the weak verbs follow them in a changed shape.

sections.heading: Reading the endings
body: Take the endings in groups. A form without an ending, or with -ַת, belongs to the singular and to the third person; the -ַת marks a feminine singular subject. A form in -וּ has a plural masculine subject. The first person is marked by -ֵת in the singular and -נָא in the plural, and does not distinguish masculine and feminine, because the speaker's gender is not shown. The second person has the long ending -ְתְּ, which is an ending in its own right: it is not a consonant of the root.

The third-person feminine plural -ָה is the rarest of these: the texts hold it only twice, in נְפַקָה (Daniel 5:5, of the fingers of a hand) and וּנְפַלָה (Daniel 7:20, of three horns). In both, a feminine plural subject asks for a feminine plural verb.

sections.heading: Which forms really occur
body: The generated tables below are filled from the words of the Aramaic of the Bible, not from a grammar. The verb הָוָא ('be, become') has the fullest set in the texts, and אֲמַר ('say') has most of the rest. A dash in a table means that no such form is found in the texts. It does not mean that the form could not exist. For instance there is no first-person plural of הָוָא, and no second-person form of אֲמַר, in the texts that survive.

Each cell of a generated table shows one real form. In the third person it shows the masculine, so the feminine forms (such as הֲוָת 'she became') are not in the grids; look for them in the table of endings and in the examples.

misunderstandings: Do not assume that every form of a verb is in the texts. The Aramaic of the Bible has about 4,800 words, so a regular verb will show only some persons of the perfect, and a form given in a grammar may simply not occur.
The third-person masculine singular (אֲמַר) is the same word as the headword. A perfect with no ending is not a stem without a subject: the subject is 'he' or whoever the sentence names.
The perfect is not an English past tense. It marks completed action as the writer sees it, and in narrative it usually tells what happened, but a sentence can be about the present or the future too.
Do not confuse the Peal perfect with the Peal participle. The participle, taught in A2.1.4, has different vowels (אָמַר against אֲמַר) and no personal ending.

deeper.heading: The first vowel
body: The Peal perfect of the strong verb usually has a shewa (or a short vowel when the first consonant is a guttural, as in אֲמַר and עֲבַד) under the first root consonant. Grammarians generally explain this as a reduction of an earlier full vowel. Aramaic has a strong tendency to reduce vowels in an open syllable before the stress, and this is one of the signs that tell Aramaic from Hebrew.

examples.analysis: שְׁאֵלְנָא (position 1) and אֲמַרְנָא (5) are both first person plural: the ending -נָא means 'we', so no pronoun is needed. The first verb has the e vowel of the stative pattern, the second the regular a. שָׂם (8) is the third person masculine singular of the verb 'set, put', with no ending: 'who gave you the decree?' The subject of this question is the unknown person, 'who'.

examples.analysis: חֲזֵיתוֹן is a second person masculine plural, 'you have seen' or, in English, 'you see'. The king speaks to the wise men. The ending -תוֹן (written -תּוּן in other places) is a second-person plural, and the root is the verb for 'see', whose last consonant is weak. A perfect of seeing or knowing is often best put in English by a present, so the perfect does not simply mean 'past'.
